english_translation: I want to rest a little before I continue forward.

dialogue.shona: Ndiri kuda kuzorora zvishoma ndisati ndaenderera mberi.
dialogue.english: I want to rest a little before I continue forward.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Ndiri [ndiri] • kuda [to / at da] • kuzorora [to / at zorora] • zvishoma [things shoma] • ndisati [ndisati] • ndaenderera [ndaenderera] • mberi [mberi]

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Saying 'If', 'When', and 'Before' ('kana' & '-sati')
grammar_notes.content: To link two events in time or condition, Shona uses 'kana' ('if / when'). When talking about a future condition ('If we work hard...'), the verb after 'kana' takes '-ka-' (e.g., 'kana tikashanda' = 'if we work'). When 'kana' sits between two nouns (like 'tsvuku kana nhema'), it simply means 'or'! To say 'before' something happens, Shona uses '-sati' ('not yet') followed by a past-form verb: 'usati wabuda' ('before you go out') or 'tisati tadya' ('before we eat').
grammar_notes.rule: kana = if / when / or | [ndisati / usati / tisati] + past verb = before [I / you / we] do something

grammar_notes.title: Infinitive Verbs & Action Nouns with 'ku-' ('kuzorora')
grammar_notes.content: Look at 'kuzorora' in this sentence. Every Shona verb in its dictionary ('to do') form begins with 'ku-': for example, 'kudya' (to eat), 'kutenga' (to buy), 'kubhadhara' (to pay), 'kuona' (to see), and 'kurwa' (to fight). Because 'ku-' verbs also behave as action nouns ('eating', 'paying', 'working'), you can attach linking prefixes directly to them: 'yekubhadhara' ('for paying'), 'pakubikwa' ('in the cooking'), and 'nekuona' ('by/with seeing').
grammar_notes.rule: ku- + Verb Stem = 'to [verb] / [verb]-ing' (ku- + -tenga = kutenga, 'to buy'; ye- + kubhadhara = yekubhadhara, 'for paying')

cultural_notes.title: Pacing Yourself on a Long Task ('Kuzorora Zvishoma')
cultural_notes.content: Taking a brief breather ('kuzorora zvishoma') before continuing forward ('ndisati ndaenderera mberi') reflects a balanced approach to long journeys and demanding physical work.

active_exercises.prompt: Translate this new polite request into English: 'Chimbomirira zvishoma pamusuwo.'
options: Come inside the house and sit on the chair.
Return home early before the sun sets.
Take your books and put them in the bag.
Please wait a little while at the door.
active_exercises.correct_answer: Please wait a little while at the door.
active_exercises.explanation: 'Chimbomirira' = 'Wait a little / for a moment right now', 'zvishoma' = 'a little', 'pamusuwo' = 'at the door'.

active_exercises.prompt: You want to politely ask an elder or a group of guests to sit down ('gara'). Which imperative form should you use?
active_exercises.explanation: Adding '-i' to the verb stem ('gara' -> 'garai') forms the plural and polite command in Shona.

active_exercises.prompt: Translate this new family sentence into English: 'Hanzvadzi yangu inoshanda muguta reHarare.'
options: My parents live at the rural homestead in Masvingo.
My sibling works in the city of Harare.
My friend passed all her school examinations this year.
The baby is sleeping quietly inside the bedroom.
active_exercises.correct_answer: My sibling works in the city of Harare.
active_exercises.explanation: 'Hanzvadzi yangu' = 'My sibling (brother/sister)', 'inoshanda' = 'works', 'muguta reHarare' = 'in the city of Harare'.
